cards.title: Zarosky Tips
cards.html:
Use guidelines (NCCN/EviQ/treatment algorithms)

Have a prepared script of what to say for standard questions

    • workup o setup o margins o doses o volumes
  • if there is a metric to assess symptoms then use it eg. I will assess their IPSS score and organise for a formal uroflow

Answer the question being asked, succinctly

  • when recommending a treatment, consider pausing to summarise to say “this pt has cancer X, stage X, risk group X. Based on “NCCN” guidelines, my recommended tx is X.”
  • dont go off on tangents about “there was a study” - examiner might have been on the study
  • questions are different difficulty levels, not always expected to know every high levels question
  • lower level = anatomy; mid = stage, options, doses; high = chemo doses, prep

If you don’t know, say you don’t know, and you would look it up. You don’t want to recommend the incorrect treatment for the pt.

Sometimes, the best dose is 0 Gy (i.e., observation)

  • know a guideline concordant dose and constraint set. multiple options, but choose one.
  • discuss the pt's case at tumour board. That's what radoncs normally do anyway :-)
  • moderate hypofractionation (vs conventional 2 Gy fractions) has become the standard of care for multiple disease sites, eg breast, prostate.
  • for some disease sites, there is a condensed formula for treatment

If you don't want to memorize dose ranges, consider picking a number in the range

Reassurance line

Most patients → short-term tiredness, hair + skin changes

Serious effects rarer

Careful monitoring & supportive management

Pt language tox

Acute side effects occur during Rx or in the few weeks afterwards and generally are temporary — the most common things are tiredness, hair loss in the treated area, and redness, dryness or peeling of the skin on the scalp, a bit like mild sunburn. Some people feel nauseous, may get mild HA, or notice ear problems like a blocked feeling, extra wax, or fluid behind the ear. Rarely, there can be seizures or swelling in the brain from radiation causing inflammation that can make existing symptoms worse.

cards.title: Additional notes
cards.html:
OARs may be used to guide the match (where appropriate) and isodose lines/contours may be used to assess OAR position and ensure tolerances are not exceeded, as per treatment priorities.

Six degrees of freedom may be corrected depending on the treatment technique, treatment machine, and departmental protocol.

Repeat pre-treatment imaging is strongly recommended when applied moves are ≥3 mm.

During-treatment (intra-fraction) imaging

Real-time intra-fraction motion management should be considered if available but is not mandated. If boosting the DIL, intra-fraction motion management is recommended.

Real-time intra-fraction motion management should be performed if reducing PTV margins to <0.3 cm.

If beam on time exceeds 3 minutes (and real-time motion management is not available), it is recommended to image between treatment beams/arcs or at agreed upon time intervals.22

If you don’t know something, don’t make up an answer to look confident (i.e. don’t guess SABR OAR constraints). It’s better to say something sensible e.g. I would reference the HyTEC papers

SRS/SABR QA

  • Every SRS/SABR plan must be QA'd by physics prior to delivery (only need to QA once unless issues)
  • QA is done using MapCHECK diode array inserted into a spherically shaped phantom (needs to be spherically shaped and not cylindrical so that you can QA non-coplanar arcs)
  • MapCHECK is a 7x7cm diode array with diodes placed 2.5mm apart (total of 784 diodes)
  • This phantom is then placed in the treatment position and treated with the plan
  • A fluence map is generated by the MapCHECK array and this is compared to the fluence map that is simulated by the treatment planning software
  • Taken from eVIQ Guidelines*

Summary

Firstly, categorise pacemaker into either Level 1, Level 2 or Level 3:

  • Level 3 = Any dependant pacemaker OR using >10MV photons (or >20MeV electrons) OR dose to pacemaker > 5Gy
  • Level 2 = Does not meet level 3 criteria AND dose to pacemaker between 2-5Gy
  • Level 1 = Does not meet level 2 or 3 criteria (i.e. dose to pacemaker < 2Gy)

Then, use precautions based on Level

  • Level 1 = Pre and post treatment pacemaker check
  • Level 2 = Add daily intrafraction HR and O2 monitoring

Level 3 = Add weekly pacemaker checks

  • Exposure to ionising radiation may lead to the malfunction of cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs).
  • The risk of CIED malfunction from ionising radiation is serious but rare.
  • When applying the CIED assessment and management strategies in this resource it is important to consider the potential impact on treatment quality or delays in commencing treatment and the subsequent risk and benefit to each individual patient and clinical scenario.
  • CIED function assessment provides patient specific CIED information including recommendations for:
    • daily monitoring of vital signs
    • daily device function alteration
  • Geometric accuracy of the fluence is more important than dosimetric accuracy with SRS/SABR QA
  • Goal is dose within 4% and geometric accuracy within 1mm

VMAT QA

  • VMAT plans should be QA'd by physics prior to first fraction (only need to

QA once unless issues)

  • QA is done using EPID (electronic portal imaging device) rather than

ArcCHECK or MapCHECK

  • A fluence map is generated by the EPID and this is compared to the fluence map that is simulated by the treatment planning software
  • Both geometric and dosimetric accuracy are important
  • Goal is dose within 3% and geometric accuracy within 2mm

3D Conformal

  • QA not usually performed
  • Only RadCalc which is a software process that
    • additional CIED function assessment.
  • Cardiologist and/or CIED technician involvement may be required to determine individual patient management strategies.
  • All patients with a CIED should have a CIED function assessment within the last 12 months prior to the commencement, and at the conclusion, of a course of radiation therapy. Some patients may require ongoing weekly CIED function assessment.
  • The use of neutron-producing beam energies is the strongest predictor of CIED malfunction.
  • Published studies and guidelines recommend doses be kept under 2-5 Gy and there is generally consensus that doses >10 Gy should be avoided.
  • Key treatment planning strategies to reduce the risk of CIED malfunction include:
    • avoiding neutron-producing beam energies
    • minimising dose to the CIED
    • avoiding the path of the planned radiation beam passing through the CIED.

Persistent fatigue.

Late toxicities (months – years post RT)

Neurocognitive decline –

Brown 2016 (JAMA): At 3 months, cognitive deterioration was more frequent with SRS+WBRT vs SRS alone (91.7% vs 63.5%, p<0.001).

Domains affected: immediate memory, delayed memory, verbal fluency.

Quality of life impact –

Soffietti 2013: WBRT after surgery or SRS negatively impacted global health status, cognitive and physical functioning, and fatigue compared to observation. Differences were clinically significant in early follow-up.

Brown 2016: SRS alone preserved overall QOL and functional independence significantly better at 3 months.

Ocular toxicity – cataract formation and, rarely, blindness if lens or optic structures exposed.

Other – chronic fatigue, persistent cognitive deficits.

Survival impact – despite improved intracranial control, WBRT did not improve OS compared to SRS alone (median OS ~7.4 vs 10.4 months, HR 1.02, NS; Brown 2016).

cards.title: Active surveillance in patient language
cards.html:
“Active Surveillance means we keep a close eye on your prostate cancer with regular blood tests,

MRI scans, and occasional repeat biopsies.

We’re recommending it because your cancer is low-risk — it’s likely to behave very slowly over many years. This approach lets us delay treatment, and the potential side effects, until it’s really necessary.

Large studies have shown that men on active surveillance have an excellent chance of living just as long as those who have immediate treatment — even out to 20 years.

Over 10 years, about half to two-thirds of men on this program eventually need treatment when the cancer shows signs of change. But that also means about one-third to one-half never need treatment at all, and can completely avoid side effects such as leakage of urine, changes in sexual function, or bowel problems.

The key is that we monitor closely, so if there are any changes, we can act early while the cancer is still very curable

cards.html:
• Who: Mostly IR/HR; not LR.
  • CF: Dose escalation: ↑ bPFS 10-20% & DMFS but ↑ G2+ GU/GI - show in multiple RCTs and 2x MA
  • OS/CSS benefit only in Gleason 8–10 (RTOG pooled).
  • DE to ≥78 Gy or using brachy/DIL boost improves bPFS/DMFS; OS gain mainly in HR Gleason 8–10.
  • Brachy boost best for IR/HR but ↑ GU tox (esp. LDR).
  • DIL boost (FLAME) → +bPFS (halves bcF 15→7%) with no ↑ late tox.
  • ADT remains essential in high-risk even with dose escalation.

Evidence

  • RCTs / MA: Multiple RCTs + 2 MA confirm ↑ bPFS, ↑ DMFS; OS benefit in HR Gleason 8–10 only.
  • RTOG 0126 / MDACC: 79 vs 70 Gy → +15–20% bPFS, slight DMFS gain, ↑ late G2 tox (≈+5%).
  • GETUG 18 (HR + LT ADT): 80 vs 70 Gy → ↑ bPFS, ↑ OS (90→95%).
  • RTOG pooled (Valicenti): Dose >66 Gy → ↑ OS/bPFS in Gleason 8–10.
  • Viani MA (7 RCTs, n=2800): ↑ bPFS, no OS/CSS gain.
  • Kalbasi JAMA: Each +2 Gy → OS ↑ ~6–7% in HR.

Approaches

  • Conventional fractionation: ≥78 Gy/39#.
  • HDR (Hoskin RCT , RADAR): ↑5/10-y bPFS 75/46% vs 61/39%.
  • DELINEATE: CF vs HF + DIL; similar tox.
  • Guidelines (EviQ): Consider isotoxic boost (e.g. 67 Gy/20#, 82–95 Gy/39#).

Non-randomized and randomized data consistently show better outcomes with multimodal approaches versus ADT alone or no local treatment.

  • Messing 2006: pN+ post-RP → immediate ADT ↑ OS, PFS, ↓ PCSM vs deferred ADT.

Suitable if AUA symptom score <15 on medication, no prior TURP/prostate surgery, no large median lobe or pubic arch interference, able to tolerate anesthesia

→ Using modern motion management and planning.

RADICAL PROSTATECTOMY +/- BILATERAL PELVIC LYMPH NODE DISSECTION

  • LND if PLN probability ≥2%; not recommended in cN+ dt limited benefit

Indication: Traditionally LR / IR organ-confined PCa; 10-yr bPFS ~70%.

  • Surgical approach: Mostly robotic; nerve-sparing possible if not T3/4, low-volume disease.
  • Advantages: Curative, complete staging, treats BPH, short course, avoids RT toxicity/second malignancy, PSA for follow-up.
  • Disadvantages: Major surgery; ED 80–100% w/o nerve-sparing (30–50% w/), stress incontinence (~30%), surgical risks.
  • Recurrence sites: Anastomosis 45%, retrovesical 15–30%, SV 20%.
  • PSA: Undetectable (<0.1 µg/L) within 1 mo; biochemical recurrence = ≥0.2 µg/L or 2 rises.
  • PLND: Staging only; no MFS/CSS/OS benefit; consider if LN+ risk ≥2–5%.

Combined/Advanced Treatments for Higher Risk Disease

  • EBRT + ADT + Brachytherapy Boost
  • ADT duration: 6 months (bulky/young) to 12 months (ASCEND-RT protocol)
  • Consider treating pelvic lymph nodes if high risk or suspicious imaging
  • Brachytherapy boost given 2–4 weeks after EBRT
  • Conventional EBRT + Long-term ADT ± Abiraterone
  • ADT duration 18–24 months (up to 24–36 months in very high risk)
  • Treat pelvic nodes if Roach score ≥15% or suspicious imaging
  • Abiraterone for node-positive or ≥2 high-risk features (cT3–4, Grade Group 4–5, PSA ≥40)

[STAMPEDE] for high risk - addiiton of abiaterone improved FFS (recommended by ASCO, ASTRO, EAU)

ADT in Prostate Cancer

Rationale

↓ clonogenic cells, ↑ radiosensitivity, ↓ prostate volume → enables DE, ↓ toxicity → Eliminates micrometastases, enhances apoptotic cell death with RT → Improved DM-FS and borderline OS benefit

Mechanisms

Hormone regulation - Testosterone production

  • LH > testes >testosterone
  • ACTH> Adrenals > DHEA >testosterone
  • Conversion to dihydrotestosterone catalysed via 5-α reductase

Acts of androgren R > prostate survival, growth, PSA secretion

Side Effects

Acute: Libido ↓, ED (80%), hot flashes (manage with venlafaxine/androcur), fatigue, mood/cognitive changes, weight gain, muscle loss, gynecomastia (reduced by 70% with 12 Gy EBRT), bone pain, metabolic changes (BMD ↓, insulin resistance, lipid changes, cardiac risks)

Late: 20% osteoporosis fractures at 5 yrs (2× risk), ↑ diabetes (50%), ischemic heart disease +20%, sudden cardiac death +15%, cognitive impairment, obesity

Management: Monitor BMD, serum calcium/VitD/PTH every 1–2 years; optimize cardiovascular health and lifestyle; smoking cessation

Timing & Protocol

Meta-analyses (RTOG + Ottawa) show starting RT + ADT simultaneously with continuation adjuvant improves DM, PFS, and BF vs neoadjuvant alone.

Addition of concurrent antiandrogen therapy improves outcomes.

STAMPEDE: 74 Gy RT + ADT 3 years ± 2 years abiraterone improves failure-free survival; ASCO recommended for nonmetastatic high-risk (N1 or ≥2 risk factors e.g., PSA >40, T3/4, Gleason 8–10).

High-risk: RT + ADT + docetaxel improves biochemical control but no OS difference at 10 years.

Recommendations by Risk Group

Low: Ø ADT (RTOG 9408 : Ø ↑ DMFS or CSS).

Favourable Intermediate: Ø No concurrent ADT (RTOG 9408 subgroup).

Unfavourable Intermediate: 4–6 months NA/CC standard (Bolla trial, RTOG 9408) = 6% 5-OS, 7% @10 yrs. Multiple RCTs ↑bPFS, DM,LF, CSS

High:18–24 months neoadjuvant/concurrent/adjuvant in dose-escalated RT era.

→ node +ve positive = recommended 36 months.

→ Addition of docetaxel Ø ↑ OS, but ↑ biochemical control.

PROSTATE SALVAGE – Viva Summary

Definitions / Biochemical Failure

  • Post-RT: ASTRO: 3 rises ((to r/o bounce), backdated to the mid point between nadir and 1st rise), Phoenix: Nadir + 2.
  • FROGG: Adjuvant = RT ≤6 mo post-RP, undetectable PSA.; Salvage = detectable/rising of any magnitude. Or PSA ≥0.1 (or imaging recurrence).

Assessment

  • Hx/Ex: Baseline GU/GI/sexual function, comorbidities, LE, DRE, prior Rx dose/fx/field, ADT, initial disease. Sx of distant mets
  • Fitness for surgery, ADT, RT
  • Review previous pathology - histo, GG, Margin, location of margins, ECE, SVI, PNI
  • PSA - see definitions above, Bounce occurs in 10-15% 2-3 years after XRT
  • Consider kinetics and initial disease eg. GG1-2 and slow DT >12 months - likley wont met/kill

Imaging

  • PSMA-PET preferred (detects at PSA 0.2–0.5; detection rates 33–95% by PSA). CT + WBBS insufficient sensitivity in asymptomatic pt with PSA <10
  • Exclude distant mets, poor sensitivity for prostate bed; Should not WH salvage bed RT in setting of negative PET
  • MRI ± biopsy for intact glands.

Adjuvant RT

  • Previously SOC for HRF (pT3/4, SM+, Gleason 8–10, SVI, ECE, pN+).
  • 3 RCTs (SWOG 8794, EORTC 22911, ARO 96-02) → ~50% ↓ bPFS; SWOG ↑ OS; but ↑ GU/GI tox.
  • Now replaced by early-salvage RT (E-SRT) in most,

  • Radiosensitive; high LR outside field → consider comprehensive fields where feasible.
  • Typical doses: 60–66Gy to primary bed; elective scalp/at-risk nodal basins 46–54Gy with boost 10–14Gy to gross bed.
  • Often combined with weekly paclitaxel in practice (no RCTs).

Pathogenesis: rapid infiltrative vascular endothelial overgrowth; VEGFR↑ → angiogenesis/leak; c-MYC amplification in RT /lymphedema-associated disease.

DDX (telangiectasia mimics): inherited (e.g., hereditary haemorrhagic telegiectasia, ATM), acquired (sun/smoking, rosacea), connective tissue disorders (SSc/CREST, SLE, DM), spider naevi (pregnancy, liver, Cushing’s, steroids), necrobiosis lipoidica, carcinoid; benign mastocytosis; injury (scar -hypertrophic or keloid, RT); malignant (BCC, Merkel, KS, cutaneous lymphomas).

  • Gloåc exception: T1: 63Gy/28Fx, T2: 65.25Gy/29Fx; (2.25Gy/fraction);

Altered Fractionation (AFx) - CRT > AFx. Use AFx only if unable to receive chemo.

  • Rationale: shorten OTT, counter repopulation, if chemo unfit
  • Hyperfractionation (HFX): 1.2 Gy BID → 80.5 Gy/7w

6 fx/wk (66–68 Gy/6w) (DAHANCA),

Key Evidence

  • MACH-NC (MA, >17k pts): Chemo +6.5% OS @5y (concurrent > induction).
  • RTOG 9003: HFX ↑ OS/LRC vs conventional; AFx ↑ acute tox.
  • DAHANCA 6/7: Acceleration (6fx/wk) ↑ LC & DFS; Ø OS.
  • GORTEC 9902 / RTOG 0129: CRT > AFx RT; Acc+CRT ≈ CRT (Ø ↑ benefit).
  • Cetuximab: better than RT alone (Bonner, biggest in OPX), but inferior to cisplatin in multiple HPV+ OPX trials (RTOG1016, De-ESCALATE).
  • Immunotherapy (IO): Ø benefit with CRT (HN004, JAVELIN, KEYNOTE-412).

Use only in metastatic/recurrent.

  • Use when: bulky/unresectable, urgent cytoreduction (airway compromise), unavoidable CRT delays, oligomet/high-met potential/ biology, organ-preservation intent.
  • Rationale: ↑ chemo early control micro met (↓DM) , potential downstaging (↓ CRT vol, ↑ organ pres if Surg), ↑ cure rates of unresectable disease
  • Common regimen: TPF (docetaxel/cisplatin/5-FU) → CRT.
  • Disadv: toxicity may delay/compromise def CRT; ↑ OTT, Ø RCT evidence of LRC/CSS/OS gain vs upfront CRT.
  • Meta-analyses/RCTs show ↓ distant mets but no consistent

LRC/CSS/OS gain over concurrent CRT.

Adjuvant RT: ↑ LRC 70vs 58% [RTOG0920] – intermediate risk

  • T4 (bone, skin, deep m tongue) – gloåc larynx

  • pN2–3 (≥3 cm or ≥2 LN)
  • DOI >4-5mm (Oral Cavity T2 with DOI >4-5mm)
  • Re-resected to negative margin
  • Relative: 3+ LN, low neck nodes, T4a primary, OC primary w/ level IV nodes.
  • Ø survival benefit with cetuximab (not a substitute)

Outcomes

CRT: <3 cm (92%), 3–6 cm (75%), >6 cm (63%).

Isolated neck recurrence rare (5–10%).

  • Neck dissection after definitive CRT: istorically planned if ≥N2, but now evidence supports surveillance if post-CRT PET negative.
  • Radical ND: Levels I–V + SCM, IJV, SAN (rare now).
  • Modified radical: Levels I–V, but preserve ≥1 structure (SCM / IJV / SAN).
  • Selective ND: Only high-risk levels (esp. cN0).
  • Lateral (II–IV) → pharynx, larynx.
  • Posterolateral (II–V).

Evidence for PET-Guided Surveillance

  • PET-NECK Trial: PET surveillance non-inferior to planned neck dissection for 5-yr LC & OS.
  • Data (Peters, Procédu, Peter Mac): PET has high NPV/PPV (>95%).
  • Low isolated neck relapse if complete response & PET-negative.
  • Even CT “residual” nodes can be observed if PET-negative.

EVIDENCE

ADJ RADIATION

RTOG 7303: PORT ↑LRC but no OS benefit.

Peters trial + MDACC (Ang): 1 RF → PORT matches LR outcomes (validates indicaBon).

SEER: PORT improved 5y OS in N+ cases (33% → 43%).

Timing: Best <6 wks postop (ideally 4–6 wks).

Dose–Response (MDACC): ≥57.6 Gy sufficient; no benefit >63 Gy unless ECE/mulB-RF; OTT impacts OS more.

RTOG 9501: Stage III/IV (≥2 LN, SM+, ENE). CRT ↑ 10-yr LRC, DFS (trend OS). Benefit confined to SM+ or ENE.

EORTC 22931: Similar design (T3/4, N2/3, SM+, PNI, LVI, lvl IV/V LN). CRT improved 5y LRC, PFS, OS.

Pooled MA: CRT ↓ LRF by ~40%, improved DFS/OS; no DM benefit; ↑ acute tox but not late tox.

RTOG 0920 (cetuximab): NegaBve. No survival benefit in IR risk.

CHEMORADIOTION

RaBonale: ↑ LRC (10% @ 2yrs), DFS (11%, 5 yrs), and OS (13% at 5 yrs) cf RT alone

Ophthalmic exam under anaesthesia with indirect ophthalmoscopy.

HIV-associated immunodeficiency appears to exert its cancer-predisposing effects through two main mechanisms: (1) reduced clearance and control of oncogenic virus infection and (2) reduced immune surveillance of malignant cells.

High viral load

Potential mechanisms are multiple and complex, involving synergism with other pro-oncogenic viruses , disruption of cell cycle regulation, blockage of tumour suppressor gene function, promotion of chromosome instability through the inhibition of telomerase activity, impairment of DNA repair function, induction of tumour angiogenesis and enhancement of the effects of exogenous carcinogens

Increased risk taking behaivour
